pedagogy.summary: Solving problems with up to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and demands careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points and equalising lengths (1.5 = 1.500), treating each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. Tasks like 'find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercise complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625). Estimation guards against place-value slips.
bestPractices: Align the decimal points and pad ragged lengths with zeros (1.500 − 0.375) so every place value lines up
Read numbers by place value all the way to thousandths
Carry and borrow across decimal columns just as with whole numbers
Use complement-to-1 reasoning (subtract from 1.000) for 'add to make 1' tasks and check by adding
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) to catch magnitude errors
keyRepresentations: Place-value columns to thousandths, aligned on the point
Measuring contexts (litres, metres) for the quantities
commonMisconceptions: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point (1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199)
Treats the decimal tail as a separate whole number ('longer is larger')
Forgets to pad and borrow across the point (1.5 − 0.375)
Complement-to-1 errors: completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the required 3 d.p. (0.4 + 0.6)

learn.summary: Solving problems with numbers to three decimal places extends place value to thousandths and depends on careful alignment. Adding and subtracting means lining up the decimal points, equalising lengths by padding with zeros (1.5 = 1.500), reading each column as ones, tenths, hundredths and thousandths, and carrying or borrowing across columns exactly as with whole numbers. 'Find two numbers to 3 d.p. that make 1' exercises complements to a whole (0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000). Estimating first guards against place-value slips.

activities.title: Column workbench: aligning and padding to thousandths
feedback: If columns are lined up by their last digits instead of the point, the sum comes out the wrong size (far from 4): re-align so tenths sit under tenths and thousandths under thousandths, padding shorter numbers with zeros.
If 1.5 is left as two digits, there is nothing to subtract the thousandths from: rewrite it as 1.500 first, then borrow across the hundredths and tenths to reach 1.125 l.
If the estimate (about 1.1) and the written answer disagree in size, a place-value slip has happened — recheck the alignment and borrowing.
activities.rationale: Place-value alignment to thousandths and borrowing across the point is the core procedural skill, and ragged-length numbers are where whole-number thinking (right-justifying, 'longer is larger') shows up; making the padding and the column structure visible turns alignment into a deliberate, checkable step. An interactive medium that snaps digits into labelled columns, shows faint ghost zeros when padding 1.500, and animates the borrow rippling left may make this mechanism concrete; these are optional illustrative supports, not required mechanisms. A static aligned-columns reference with tap-to-reveal place values can model a single worked calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems, so it suits review rather than independent practice.
sourceClaims: Decimal size and calculation depend on place value, and errors arise from whole-number thinking (treating the decimal tail as a separate whole number, 'longer is larger'); ragged-length decimals are essential for revealing these errors, whereas tidy same-length items let faulty rules pass.
learnerActions: Set out the subtraction 1.5 − 0.375 in place-value columns (ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths) aligned on the decimal point — the measuring context is a 1.5-litre bottle from which 0.375 l is poured out, finding how much is left.
Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500 by writing zeros in the empty hundredths and thousandths columns before subtracting.
Carry out the subtraction, borrowing just as with whole numbers (from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths), to reach 1.125 l remaining.
Add the three ragged measurements 1.2 m + 0.567 m + 2.233 m by first aligning on the point and padding every number to the same length (1.2 = 1.200), then summing each column to get 4.000 m.
Estimate first (1.5 − 0.375 ≈ 1.5 − 0.4 ≈ 1.1) and check the answer's size against the estimate.
activities.intendedInsight: 1.5 and 1.500 are the same number, but writing the padding zeros makes the hundredths and thousandths columns available so the digits line up and the borrow can ripple from the tenths through the hundredths to the thousandths.

activities.title: Make 1: complements to a whole at three decimal places
feedback: If a pair like 0.375 + 0.735 is chosen, each column was completed to 10 separately (that pair totals 1.110, not 1): instead subtract the whole number 1.000 − 0.375 to get 0.625, then add to check the total is exactly 1.000.

If the total comes to 0.999 or similar, each column (including the thousandths) was probably completed to 9, giving 0.624 instead of 0.625. Only the thousandths should make 10, with the tenths and hundredths making 9 because of the carries, so that the total is one whole, written 1.000.
If a pair is not written to three decimal places, rewrite it to 3 d.p. and confirm it still totals 1.000.
activities.rationale: Complement-to-1 tasks rehearse decomposing a whole and expose the common error of completing each column to ten. Checking by adding back links the complement to addition and reinforces that the parts must reconstitute exactly one whole. A bar/length model where the two parts must fill one whole may make 'completing the whole' felt as a length; it is an optional illustrative support, not a required medium.
learnerActions: Given 0.375, find the second number to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.000, by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625).
Check the pair by adding the two numbers back together and confirming they total exactly 1.000.
Explain why 0.4 + 0.6, though it equals 1, does not meet the 'three decimal places' requirement, and give a valid 3-d.p. pair (such as 0.001 + 0.999).
Optionally model the complement as two lengths placed end to end along a bar representing one whole, where only the correct pair closes the gap with no gap or overlap and a running total shows 1.000.
activities.intendedInsight: A complement to 1 is found by subtracting from the whole written as 1.000, not by completing each column to 10 independently; the two parts together must make exactly one whole.

constraints: Use ragged-length decimals (different numbers of decimal places) in practice, not only tidy same-length items: equal-length items can let faulty right-justify or 'longer is larger' rules pass undetected.

A static aligned-columns picture or tap-to-reveal reference can illustrate one calculation but does not enforce alignment on new problems; reserve it for modelling or review and require learners to lay out and compute fresh problems themselves.

Multiple-choice or fill-in checks can diagnose misalignment and complement errors but assess recognition of a final value; independent construction requires learners to set out the columns, pad, and carry/borrow themselves.
Insist complements be written to the required three decimal places (reject 0.4 + 0.6 for a 3-d.p. task even though it sums to 1).

When writing distractors for 1.5 − 0.375, the correct answer is 1.125; plausible error-based distractors include 1.275 (subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in each column instead of borrowing) and 1.225 (borrowing without reducing the tenths digit from 5 to 4). Include 1.125 once as the correct option, and make sure no distractor equals it.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources have not been re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Self-audit of arithmetic: 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 = 4.000; 1.500 − 0.375 = 1.125; 1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625; 0.375 + 0.625 = 1.000 and 0.001 + 0.999 = 1.000 — all verified correct. The original row's complement-error example (0.375 + 0.725 = 1.100) is intentionally used only as an error to diagnose, never as a correct answer.

The source claim supports using ragged-length decimals to reveal place-value errors; it does not establish comparative efficacy of any particular medium (interactive columns vs. picture vs. quiz). Medium recommendations are framed as affordances/limits, not necessity.

The legacy claim that depth/3D 'adds nothing' and that in-role dialogue cannot carry the insight were catalog fit judgements, not established facts; softened or omitted rather than asserted as universal laws.

The litre/bottle measuring context for 1.5 − 0.375 and the metre context for the three-measurement sum are retained to preserve the row's concrete measuring representations; the 'number line to thousandths' representation from the pedagogy field was not expanded into an activity.

probeDeeper: Before adding, roughly what should 1.234 + 0.567 + 2.199 be near — more or less than 4? Why?
Do 0.4 and 0.6 have three decimal places? Give me a pair written to 3 d.p. that makes exactly 1.
How can you check that your two numbers really add to exactly 1?

errorPatterns.pattern: Right-justifies ragged decimals instead of aligning the point — lines up 1.234, 0.567, 2.199 by their last digits
errorPatterns.nextMove: Align on the decimal point and pad shorter numbers with zeros so tenths sit under tenths, thousandths under thousandths.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Columns don't match place value; the sum is the wrong size (not near 4)

errorPatterns.pattern: Fails to pad and borrow across the point — tackles 1.5 − 0.375 without rewriting 1.500, botching the borrow
errorPatterns.nextMove: Rewrite 1.5 as 1.500, then subtract with borrowing across the hundredths and tenths just as in whole-number subtraction.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 1.175 or 1.235; leaves 1.5 as two digits and cannot subtract thousandths from nothing

errorPatterns.pattern: Complement-to-1 error — completes each column to 10 independently (0.375 + 0.725) or ignores the 3-d.p. requirement (0.4 + 0.6)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Find the complement by subtracting from 1.000 (1.000 − 0.375 = 0.625) and check by adding; stress the whole is 1.000, not 0.999 or ten in each column.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The chosen pair does not total exactly 1.000, or is not to three decimal places

responseLevels.gap: Right-justifies ragged decimals; cannot borrow across the point; gives complements that don't total 1.
responseLevels.full: Aligns on the point and pads ragged lengths, adds and subtracts to 3 d.p. with correct borrowing (4.000; 1.125), finds a valid 3-d.p. complement to 1, and estimates to check; transfers to a new problem.
responseLevels.partial: Adds/subtracts equal-length decimals correctly but misaligns ragged ones or forgets to pad, or finds a 'make 1' pair only when it is tidy (0.5 + 0.5) rather than to 3 d.p.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Say: 'Show me your method for each. First, add 1.234 m + 0.567 m + 2.199 m. Second, a 1.5-litre bottle has 0.375 litres poured out — how much is left? Third, find two numbers, each with three decimal places, that add up to exactly 1.' Watch how they line the numbers up and handle the borrow.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The ragged sum (three different lengths) exposes right-justify misalignment; 1.5 − 0.375 forces padding to 1.500 and a borrow across the point; 'make 1' to 3 d.p. exposes complement errors (many write 0.375 + 0.725, completing each column to 10). A child who aligns on the point, pads with zeros and borrows correctly gets 4.000, 1.125 and a valid complement; a misaligner or column-completer does not.
